findings.explanation: escapeDomain uses String.replace with a string pattern, which escapes only the first '.'. For a configured domain with two or more dots, such as 'eu.pay.example', the regex becomes '...eu\.pay.example$', where the second dot matches any character. An origin such as 'https://eu.pay-example' then passes isAllowed although it is not the configured domain or a subdomain of it, which breaks the exact-match contract.

toPence multiplies by 100 in binary floating point and then truncates. For amount 19.99, 19.99 * 100 is 1998.9999999999998, so Math.trunc returns 1998 pence instead of the 1999 the contract requires. Splitting such amounts then sums to the wrong total.

hasMore uses end < items.length - 1 where it should use end < items.length. For items [1,2,3] with pageSize 2, page 1 reports hasMore false although element 3 remains. collectAll then returns [1,2] and drops the final element. The same off-by-one drops the last element of any array whose length is a multiple of pageSize, such as [1,2] with pageSize 1.

hasRole calls includes on the value of user.role when that value is a string, which performs a substring match rather than an exact role comparison. A user with role 'co-owner' satisfies hasRole(user, 'owner') and therefore canManageBilling, and a role such as 'not-analyst' satisfies hasRole(user, 'analyst'). The contract requires exact equality.

deposit adds amount to balance without checking the result. A balance of 9007199254740990 with a deposit of 5 gives 9007199254740995, which is not a safe integer. The call returns normally and records the history entry, but the contract requires it to throw and leave balance unchanged in this case.

The SORT_PATTERN regex uses the m flag, so ^ and $ match at line boundaries. A sort value such as 'name\n1; DROP TABLE orders' passes the test because its first line is exactly 'name'. The whole string is then appended to ORDER BY, which lets attacker-controlled text reach the SQL text. The contract requires a throw for any ORDER BY content beyond the allowed columns and ASC/DESC.

The check rejects only values starting with '//'. A value such as '/\evil.example' passes, because the WHATWG parser treats a backslash as a slash for special schemes and resolves it against https://app.example to https://evil.example/. A value such as '/\t/evil.example' also passes, because the parser strips the tab and the result is protocol-relative. Either input sends the user to an external origin, which the contract forbids.
